nameStory: The name 'betony' comes from the ancient Celtic word 'bew' meaning head, referring to its traditional use in treating headaches. It's called 'hedge-nettle' because it often grows along hedgerows and has somewhat nettle-like leaves, though it won't sting you like true nettles do!
description: Common hedge-nettle is a sturdy perennial herb that grows 1-3 feet tall with a distinctly square stem typical of the mint family. It produces dense spikes of tubular purple-pink flowers that sit atop the plant like a crown. The wrinkled, heart-shaped leaves have scalloped edges and grow in opposite pairs along the stem. Originally from Europe, this plant is quite rare in New England but occasionally pops up in gardens or naturalized areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, cylindrical spikes of tubular purple-pink flowers cluster at the top of stems, with each individual bloom having a hooded upper lip and three-lobed lower lip

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with deeply wrinkled surfaces and scalloped edges feel rough and textured, arranged in opposite pairs along the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as an upright clump 1-3 feet tall with multiple square stems that feel distinctly four-sided when rolled between your fingers

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Square stems are characteristic of the mint family - you can easily feel the four distinct corners when you gently squeeze the stem

habitat: In its native Europe, betony thrives in grasslands, woodland edges, and hedgerows on well-drained soils. In New England, it's extremely rare and most likely found in old garden sites, abandoned homesteads, or areas where it has escaped cultivation. Look for it in partially shaded spots with moderately fertile, not-too-wet soil.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as wrinkled, heart-shaped leaves in basal rosettes close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Flowering stems shoot up in mid to late summer, topped with distinctive purple-pink flower spikes that bloom from bottom to top over several weeks.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and leaves may turn yellowish before dying back, with seeds developing in small nutlets within the old flower spikes.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no above-ground trace until spring.

funFact: Medieval herbalists believed betony was so powerful it could protect against evil spirits and witchcraft - they even had a saying 'sell your coat and buy betony' to emphasize its supposed magical and medicinal value!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other members of the mint family like wild bergamot or heal-all, but betony's dense, cylindrical flower spike sitting like a crown on top of the plant is distinctive. Unlike heal-all's compact purple clusters, betony's flowers form a tall, narrow spike.
contextualKnowledge: This plant was recently moved from the genus Stachys (hedge-nettles) to its own genus Betonica based on genetic studies. You might still see it listed as Stachys officinalis in older field guides. The name 'officinalis' indicates it was once considered an official medicinal plant.
compareHints: Since betony is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it to its close relatives in the mint family. Unlike other hedge-nettles (Stachys species) which have flowers scattered along the stem, betony concentrates all its flowers in a single dense spike at the very top. The leaves are also more distinctly heart-shaped and wrinkled than most other mint family members.
